title: Sadat Goes to Jerusalem
text:
In 1977 Egypt and Israel had fought four wars in less than thirty years. No Arab leader recognized Israel, and talks on a Middle East settlement were stuck in procedural arguments.

On 9 November 1977, in a speech to the Egyptian parliament, President Anwar Sadat said that he was ready to go to the ends of the earth for peace, even to the Knesset in Jerusalem. Many listeners took it as rhetoric. Israel's prime minister, Menachem Begin, responded with an official invitation. Ten days later, on 19 November, Sadat's plane landed at Ben Gurion airport, and the next day he addressed the Knesset. He did not soften his demands: Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories and a solution for the Palestinians. But by coming in person he broke the taboo of direct recognition and changed the atmosphere completely.

Negotiations that followed were difficult and nearly failed. In September 1978 President Jimmy Carter brought Sadat and Begin to Camp David for thirteen days of talks, which produced the Camp David Accords. On 26 March 1979 Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty, and Israel returned the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt in stages. Sadat and Begin shared the Nobel Peace Prize for 1978.

The gamble cost Sadat dearly in the Arab world. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League, and in October 1981 Sadat was assassinated by Islamist officers. The peace between Egypt and Israel has held.
lesson: A bold, personal gesture can break a deadlock that years of procedure could not. Be prepared to pay a price for it, and keep your substantive demands clear.
people: Anwar Sadat, Menachem Begin, Jimmy Carter
source: Sadat's speech to the Knesset (20 November 1977); Jimmy Carter, Keeping Faith (1982); Lawrence Wright, Thirteen Days in September (2014)
